title: Beyond Tomorrow

evidence.note: The Internet Archive item is dated 1940. A 1940 US film is free only if its notice was missing or its copyright was not renewed. I found no primary record either way: no renewal-absence result and no notice-failure document. The uploader says they own no rights and believe the film is public domain. That is a belief, not a rights determination.
This is a sound film. The recorded track normally shares the film's own copyright status, so the score is undetermined for the same reason as the print. I found no separate music-copyright record.

The Internet Archive metadata credits an original story by Mildred Cram and Adele Comandini, with a screenplay by Adele Comandini. I did not find whether the story was published separately or when, so its term is unconfirmed.

The Internet Archive metadata says a colorized version was produced by Legend Films in 2004. A faithful black-and-white copy adds no new US copyright (Bridgeman v. Corel). The colorization, and any added material, can carry its own protection.

editorial:
Beyond Tomorrow is a 1940 fantasy film directed by A. Edward Sutherland and produced by Lee Garmes. The story is credited to Mildred Cram and Adele Comandini, and Comandini wrote the screenplay. Three elderly industrialists die in an airplane crash and come back as ghosts to reunite a young couple. The uploader calls it a little-remembered Christmas film, which makes it a natural seasonal pick.

I could not confirm the print's status from a primary record. A 1940 film is free in the US only if its notice was missing or its copyright was not renewed. The print, score, story and trademark layers therefore stay undetermined. The rights trap is the Internet Archive upload itself. The uploader says they own no rights and believe the film is public domain, and a belief is not a rights check. The upload is also described as digitally remastered by the National Film Museum, Incorporated. Check the 1967 to 1969 renewal catalogs before reusing it.
faq: Is Beyond Tomorrow (1940) free to use?

Not confirmed. It is a 1940 film, so it is free only if its notice was missing or its copyright was not renewed. I could not verify either from a primary record. Check the 1967-1969 renewal catalogs using the links in the dossier. The uploader's public-domain statement on the Internet Archive is not a rights determination.
Does a copy on the Internet Archive prove the film is public domain?
No. Anyone can upload a film to the Internet Archive and label it public domain. The label is not a rights check. The renewal records are what decide it.
